tldr: This paper proposes KILVO, a state estimation framework for humanoid robots that tightly couples joint encoders (kinematics), an IMU, a LiDAR, and a camera. Achieving both a high output rate of 1 kHz and high-precision localization and mapping, it was verified on a real robot to exhibit seamless degradation and recovery robustness even during sensor failures or degradation.
hero_caption: Overall system architecture of KILVO. Centered on a hybrid ESIKF combining a 1 kHz asynchronous phase (kinematic updates) and a 10 Hz sequential phase (LiDAR and visual updates), it cleanly integrates contact estimation and modality switching in response to sensor failures.
overview:
High-frequency, high-precision state estimation is essential for the control and autonomous navigation of humanoid robots. Traditionally, kinematics-based odometry using IMUs and joint encoders has been mainstream, but it suffered from rapid drift accumulation caused by severe foot-strike impacts and foot slippage. Recently, SLAM integrating LiDAR and cameras has emerged, yet it had a fatal vulnerability: systems often collapsed when sensor data dropped out due to intense humanoid-specific vibrations, fall risks, or outdoor illumination changes.

To solve this, the authors developed KILVO, an odometry system integrating four onboard sensor types—encoders, IMU, LiDAR, and camera—that withstands aggressive motions and sensor failures. At its core is an "asynchronous-sequential hybrid process" based on an error-state iterated Kalman filter (ESIKF). Building on IMU state predictions, it incorporates leg kinematic constraints from encoders asynchronously at an ultra-high rate of 1 kHz, while sequentially integrating exteroceptive LiDAR and camera data arriving at 10 Hz to suppress drift. Furthermore, without mounting extra force sensors on the feet, the authors built a contact estimation module using existing data and an automatic fallback mechanism that transitions to optimal degraded modes during sensor loss.

Extensive experiments on a physical robot (Unitree G1) and public datasets showed that KILVO maintains a 1 kHz output rate suitable for control loops while outperforming state-of-the-art methods in estimation accuracy. Even in harsh scenarios where cameras or LiDAR abruptly fail during locomotion, it proved capable of autonomously switching modes and continuing walking without estimation failure.
contributions: Proposed an asynchronous-sequential hybrid ESIKF framework that tightly couples leg kinematics, IMU, LiDAR, and camera, achieving both a 1 kHz high-rate output and adaptability to sensor failures.
Developed a contact estimation module that accurately determines foot contact using existing kinematic-inertial data and a voxel map, without requiring dedicated contact or force sensors.
Constructed and released a comprehensive humanoid SLAM dataset comprising 15 real-robot sequences covering diverse gaits, rough terrain, and sensor degradation scenarios.
Demonstrated estimation accuracy surpassing state-of-the-art fusion SLAM methods and outstanding fault resilience through public dataset evaluations and physical humanoid experiments.

sections.heading: How to Build Drift-Free, Failure-Resilient State Estimation on a Shaky Humanoid
sections.summary: Humanoid robots are harsh platforms prone to sensor observation noise and data dropouts caused by foot impacts and strong vibrations. This section introduces the goals and contributions of KILVO, an odometry framework that tightly integrates encoders, IMU, LiDAR, and camera with high output frequency and strong fault tolerance.
sections.details:
In recent years, humanoid robot hardware performance has improved rapidly, but accurate state estimation (odometry) is indispensable for stable locomotion in unknown environments. To obtain low-latency control inputs, kinematics-based estimation using IMUs and joint encoders has been widely used. However, due to the upright bipedal structure, foot contact is inherently unstable, causing position and yaw drift to accumulate rapidly over long distances and on complex terrain.

Exteroceptive SLAM integrating LiDAR and cameras has also advanced, but humanoid-specific challenges stand in the way. Severe body vibrations from walking impacts, aggressive optical flow, and featureless or textureless environments routinely cause sensor degradation or data packet drops. Conventional SLAM algorithms assume uninterrupted sensor streams, meaning the loss of a single sensor can cause the entire system to diverge.

Furthermore, effectively utilizing leg kinematic constraints requires accurate contact information to know which foot is on the ground. However, mounting extra force/torque (F/T) sensors on the feet introduces hardware cost and reliability concerns. To resolve all these issues, this work proposes KILVO, an integrated framework using only standard onboard sensors that achieves both 1 kHz high-rate output and sensor failure resilience via an asynchronous-sequential hybrid filter.

captions.F1: Overview of the standard onboard sensors equipped on humanoid robots and the operational modalities provided by KILVO. Depending on sensor availability, it adapts seamlessly from the full KILV mode to KI (LiDAR loss), LIV (encoder loss), and others.

sections.heading: The Evolution of Humanoid SLAM, Multimodal Fusion, and Contact Estimation
sections.summary: This section reviews related work across three areas: humanoid state estimation, robust multimodal SLAM fusion, and contact estimation. It highlights that many existing methods assume fixed sensor suites and ideal environments, lacking dynamic adaptation to sensor dropouts and freedom from specialized hardware.
sections.details:
Related research is broadly categorized into three fields:

- Humanoid Odometry: Early approaches mainly relied on proprioceptive estimation using IMUs and joint encoders via error-state Kalman filters (ESKF) or invariant observers. However, because position and yaw are unobservable, drift is inevitable. While subsequent research integrated cameras and LiDAR, systems that tightly couple all four sensors (encoders, IMU, LiDAR, and camera) while delivering high-rate outputs suitable for control have been extremely rare.

- Robust Multimodal SLAM: Methods fusing multiple exteroceptive sensors include R3LIVE and factor graph optimization (FGO)-based frameworks. However, most existing works only handle measurement noise degradation, not total sensor loss or online estimator reconfiguration. Furthermore, FGO carries a heavy computational burden, making it unsuitable for the 1 kHz low-latency feedback required by low-level humanoid controllers.

- Contact Estimation: Foot contact detection has traditionally relied on ground reaction force (GRF) thresholding or deep learning classifiers. Yet, GRF thresholding is sensitive to surface changes, and deep learning models struggle to generalize to unseen gaits and terrain. A contact estimation module was attempted in the prior work HR2-KILO, but it suffered from limitations such as coupled false positives between both feet and strong dependence on LiDAR point clouds.

sections.heading: A Smart Architecture Combining Asynchronous and Sequential Phases
sections.summary: This section describes the overall processing pipeline of KILVO. It features a two-tier structure: a 1 kHz asynchronous phase that immediately applies leg kinematic constraints to output states, and a 10 Hz sequential phase that consecutively incorporates LiDAR and visual observations to correct drift.
sections.details:
The overall architecture of KILVO is clean and well-structured. Upon receiving input from joint encoders (1 kHz), the IMU (200 Hz), the LiDAR (10 Hz), and the camera (10 Hz), a health status checker monitors sensor availability and data quality in real time.

When all sensors function normally, the system updates states in a hybrid manner using an error-state iterated Kalman filter (ESIKF):

- Prediction Step: Uses IMU measurements to forward-predict prior distributions of robot orientation, position, and velocity at a high frequency.
- Asynchronous Phase (1 kHz): Uses forward kinematics constraints of the legs from encoders to compute residuals and immediately update the state. This latest updated state is directly output to controllers at 1 kHz while also being stored in a state buffer for downstream processing.
- Sequential Phase (10 Hz): When a LiDAR scan arrives, it uses the trajectory in the state buffer to undistort points with high accuracy. A LiDAR update is executed first using point-to-plane residuals against a voxel map. Retaining this geometric prior, a visual update follows consecutively using direct photometric errors from camera images.

Geometric structures and visual reference patches are centrally managed in a shared hash-indexed voxel map. Moreover, this map is shared with the contact estimation module, completely eliminating redundant computations throughout the system.

sections.heading: Mathematical Formulation of the Hybrid ESIKF and Degraded Modes for Sensor Failures
sections.summary: This section details the equations and algorithms covering state prediction, high-rate leg kinematic updates, sequential LiDAR/camera updates, and mode transitions during sensor loss. It introduces dynamic covariance reweighting based on foot impact magnitude.
sections.details:
The state vector contains the body orientation ${}^{W}\mathbf{R}_{I}$, position ${}^{W}\mathbf{p}_{I}$, velocity ${}^{W}\mathbf{v}_{I}$, IMU biases, contact foot positions ${}^{W}\mathbf{p}_{c}$, and the camera inverse exposure time $\tau$.

IV-A & IV-B (State Definition and Prediction): Propagates covariances on manifolds using discrete-time process models driven by the latest IMU measurements.

IV-C (Asynchronous Phase): Constructs an observation model consisting of three geometric constraints—foot velocity, position, and height—for the contact foot. A key contribution is "foot-strike impact adaptation." To avoid corruption by large impact shock at touchdown, a normalized residual deviation score $\mathbf{d}_{r}$ is computed to dynamically scale up the nominal measurement covariance $\mathcal{R}_{c}^{nom}$, adjusting constraint reliability.

IV-D (Sequential Phase): In the LiDAR update, points are undistorted using the high-rate state buffer from the asynchronous phase. The ESIKF is then iteratively updated using point-to-plane geometric residuals. In the visual update, points from the voxel map are projected onto the image plane to perform direct alignment via photometric errors against reference patches. Because the posterior state from the LiDAR update acts as a strong prior for the visual update, alignment converges extremely reliably.

IV-E (Multimodal Adaptation): When sensor timestamps stall beyond a threshold, or when spatial point cloud degeneration or feature loss is detected, the system immediately switches to the corresponding degraded modality (e.g., KILV with all sensors, KI without LiDAR, LIV without encoders). For instance, if LiDAR fails, a virtual ground patch is fitted from historical contact foot positions, sustaining kinematics-based contact estimation and state updates without a point cloud map. Upon recovery, the system safely transitions back to full mode once foot-strike shocks subside.

sections.heading: Accurate Foot Touchdown and Liftoff Detection with Zero Extra Sensors
sections.summary: This section details the contact estimation module, which detects bipedal contact accurately without force sensors by using only IMU acceleration, kinematic foot velocity, and foot clearance from the voxel map.
sections.details:
V-A (Dynamic Initialization): Obtains static statistics $\mathcal{S}^{st}$ during stationary initialization and dynamically computes baseline statistics $\mathcal{S}^{sw}$ for acceleration, foot velocity, and kinematic residuals during the initial swing phase after walking starts. It also extracts a local ground patch near the feet from the map and maintains a sliding window $\mathcal{C}$ of foot clearance history. To handle initial blind zones lacking surrounding LiDAR points, a ground plane is estimated using the stance foot and virtual anchor points.

V-B (Contact / Non-Contact Determination): Monitors dimensionless acceleration deviation $d_{a}$ and foot velocity deviation $d_{fv}$. When an acceleration cue triggers while a foot is swinging (non-contact), it compares the area trajectories of the clearance windows $\mathcal{C}_{i}$ and assigns contact to the foot that finished swinging and reached the ground. When foot velocity drops, contact is also identified via the downward clearance trend from linear regression.

In physical environments, impact shock vibrates sensor signals on both feet, easily causing false detections. KILVO introduces a "hysteresis mechanism": a foot marked in contact is forbidden from liftoff until acceleration settles, and a swinging foot cannot trigger contact until its velocity peak passes. This drastically suppresses chattering.

sections.heading: Unitree G1 Real-Robot Locomotion Tests and Sensor Stress Testing
sections.summary: The system was rigorously evaluated across 15 sequences on public datasets and a physical Unitree G1 robot for accuracy, efficiency, and fault resilience. It outperformed state-of-the-art methods at 1 kHz output rates, remaining stable through mid-run sensor failures and harsh terrain.
sections.details:
VI-A & VI-B (Experimental Setup and Contact Evaluation): Evaluated on a desktop PC and an onboard Jetson Orin NX. In contact evaluation on public datasets against ground reaction force (GRF) thresholding, deep learning (DCE), and prior work (HRC), KILVO achieved the highest accuracy and lowest false-positive rate (mean FPR of 3.67%) across 7 of 8 sequences. Reusing ground patches per contact event reduced computation time from 0.08–0.09 ms (HRC) to about 0.02 ms (~76% reduction).

VI-C (Accuracy Evaluation): Compared against LIO-SAM, FAST-LIO2, LIKO, and HR2-KILO on LIKO and HR2-KILO datasets. KILVO achieved the lowest absolute trajectory error (mean RMSE 0.0151 m) and relative error in most sequences, keeping end-point Z-axis error under 1 cm. In physical G1 experiments (Table V), it achieved the best accuracy with an average end translation error of 0.0145 m across all 15 sequences. While aggressive locomotion caused feature tracking failures in LIO-SAM and R3LIVE, KILVO maintained very stable trajectories.

VI-D (Computational Efficiency): Total average processing time was approximately 14 ms. Kinematic updates took less than 0.2 ms each (satisfying 1 kHz), LiDAR processing took ~10 ms, and visual processing took ~5 ms. Despite tightly coupling four sensors, it never disrupts real-time control loops.

VI-E (Robustness Stress Tests): Tested under harsh conditions where sensors were lost mid-run. During a >9-minute outdoor sequence, camera and LiDAR were sequentially cut; the system smoothly degraded from KILV → KIL → KI, successfully returning to the origin using only encoders and IMU for contact estimation and locomotion (end translation error of 0.3338 m). In temporary sensor drop and recovery tests, it also returned to full mode smoothly without state jumps.

sections.heading: Summary and Future Outlook
sections.summary: KILVO combines leg kinematics, IMU, LiDAR, and camera for humanoid odometry, delivering high accuracy, high frequency, and strong robustness. Future extensions aim to integrate learning-based modules.
sections.details:
This paper presented KILVO, a state estimation framework that fully exploits standard humanoid onboard sensors. By employing an asynchronous-sequential hybrid ESIKF, it achieves both a 1 kHz high output rate and high-precision exteroceptive drift correction, supported by a lightweight contact estimation module requiring no extra hardware.

Furthermore, by incorporating an adaptive mechanism that switches modalities smoothly and without interruption during real-world sensor failures or degradation, the framework proves capable of sustaining autonomous humanoid locomotion under harsh conditions. The source code and datasets have been released to the community. Looking forward, the authors plan to incorporate learning-based scene perception modules into KILVO to further enhance adaptability.

takeaways: Processing sensors with vastly different rates (1 kHz encoders vs. 10 Hz LiDAR/camera) via an asynchronous-sequential hybrid ESIKF is an extremely practical and effective design.
Without external force sensors, combining IMU acceleration, kinematic foot velocity, and voxel map foot clearance enables accurate (>95%) and lightweight (0.02 ms) contact detection.
Beyond simply fusing sensors, explicitly designing degraded fallback modes specifying which geometric and kinematic constraints remain is vital for physical humanoid survival.
Using normalized residual deviations to adaptively scale up kinematic measurement covariances during foot-strike impacts is highly effective at mitigating shock-induced noise.
limitations: If exteroceptive sensors like LiDAR and cameras drop out for prolonged durations, proprioception alone (KI mode) cannot fundamentally prevent long-term position and yaw drift.
Because contact estimation relies on local ground patch fitting, accuracy may degrade on severely slipping surfaces or unstable ground like loose stepping stones and shifting tiles.

In the visual odometry module, maximum exposure time is kept short to prevent motion blur from foot-strike shocks, limiting robustness in extreme low-light environments or abrupt illumination changes.
